original_question: Does the gene on the X chromosome, which when mutated is associated with Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome, include an ATPase/helicase domain?

final_qi.question: Does the gene on the X chromosome, which when mutated is associated with Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome, include an ATPase/helicase domain?
final_qi.long_answer: Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome is now known to be the same clinical entity as Börjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome.  Pathogenic variants that cause this X-linked syndrome occur in the PHF6 gene located at Xq26.2.  The PHF6 protein is a nuclear protein that contains two PHD-type zinc-finger domains and several nuclear-localisation signals, but it does not possess the Walker A/B motifs, RecA-like fold or other structural elements that define ATP-dependent helicase/ATPase domains.  Therefore, the gene implicated in Smith-Fineman-Myers syndrome does not encode an ATPase/helicase domain.

final_answer.long_answer: The X-linked gene mutated in Smith–Fineman–Myers (ATR-X) syndrome is ATRX, a member of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling family. The ATRX protein contains a conserved C-terminal SNF2-type ATPase/helicase domain that supplies ATP-dependent DNA unwinding and chromatin-remodeling activity. Hence, the gene clearly includes an ATPase/helicase domain.
